title: Tokens: turning text into numbers
summary: A model only does arithmetic, so text is first cut into tokens and each token gets an integer ID. Characters give a tiny vocabulary but long sequences; whole words give short sequences but a huge vocabulary and unknown words. Byte pair encoding sits in between: start from characters (or bytes) and repeatedly merge the most frequent neighbouring pair.
llm_link: Every prompt you send to an LLM is first split into tokens by a BPE-style tokenizer, and the model's output is a choice among those same token IDs. Context limits and API prices are counted in tokens, not words, which is why a rare word or another language can cost more.
key_ideas: A tokenizer has two halves: encode (text to a list of integer IDs) and decode (IDs back to text).
Character tokens: tiny vocabulary, long sequences, nothing is ever unknown.
Word tokens: short sequences, huge vocabulary, and unseen words collapse to an <unk> placeholder.
Byte pair encoding: count neighbouring pairs, merge the most frequent pair into a new token, repeat. Common words become one token; rare words become a few familiar pieces.
A token ID is a name tag, not a quantity. The model turns each ID into a vector (next lesson).

quiz.q: Character-level tokenization of a text whose distinct characters are ' ', 'd', 'e', 'h', 'l', 'o', 'r', 'w' (sorted, IDs 0-7). Predict the result of encoding "hold".
quiz.explain: Each character's ID is its position in the sorted vocabulary: h is 3, o is 5, l is 4, d is 1.

quiz.q: Why does a word-level tokenizer struggle with a word it never saw during training?
options: It splits the word into characters automatically
The word has no ID, so it becomes a generic <unk> token and its meaning is lost
It gives the word the ID of the most similar word
quiz.explain: A word vocabulary is fixed after training. Anything outside it can only be mapped to a placeholder, which carries no information about the actual word.

quiz.q: One BPE step on the token list [a, b, a, b, c, a, b]: which pair is merged first?
quiz.explain: Counting neighbouring pairs: (a,b) appears 3 times, (b,a) once, (b,c) once, (c,a) once. BPE merges the most frequent pair.

quiz.q: Why do modern tokenizers like GPT-2's start BPE from bytes rather than characters?
options: With 256 starting byte tokens, any text in any script can be encoded, so nothing is unknown
Bytes carry more meaning than characters
It makes the vocabulary smaller than a character vocabulary
quiz.explain: UTF-8 writes every character, accent or emoji as one to four bytes. If all 256 byte values are in the starting vocabulary, every possible string can be encoded.

quiz.q: An LLM API bills you by tokens. Which text is likely to use the most tokens for the same number of characters?
options: A random string of rare names and symbols
They all use the same number
quiz.explain: Common words were merged into single tokens during BPE training. Rare strings fall back to small pieces, so they need more tokens per character.

problems.title: A character tokenizer
problems.prompt:
Build the simplest tokenizer from the video.

  • build_vocab(text) returns the sorted list of distinct characters in text.
  • encode(s, vocab) returns the list of IDs, where a character's ID is its position in vocab.
  • decode(ids, vocab) turns IDs back into a string.
vocab = build_vocab("hello world")   # [' ', 'd', 'e', 'h', 'l', 'o', 'r', 'w']
encode("hello", vocab)              # [3, 2, 4, 4, 5]
decode([3, 2, 4, 4, 5], vocab)       # 'hello'

tests.name: vocabulary is sorted and distinct
tests.code:
v = build_vocab('hello world')
assert v == [' ', 'd', 'e', 'h', 'l', 'o', 'r', 'w'], f'expected the 8 distinct characters in sorted order, got {v}. A set removes duplicates; sorted() orders it and returns a list.'

tests.name: encodes hello
tests.code:
v = build_vocab('hello world')
out = encode('hello', v)
assert out == [3, 2, 4, 4, 5], f'expected [3, 2, 4, 4, 5], got {out}. Each ID is the position of the character in the sorted vocabulary.'

tests.name: decodes back
tests.code:
v = build_vocab('hello world')
out = decode([3, 2, 4, 4, 5], v)
assert out == 'hello', f'expected the string hello, got {out!r}. decode should return a str, not a list: use "".join(...).'

tests.name: round trip on any text
tests.code:
t = 'the cat sat on the mat'
v = build_vocab(t)
assert decode(encode(t, v), v) == t, 'decode(encode(t)) should give back exactly the original text'

tests.name: spaces count as characters
tests.code:
v = build_vocab('a b')
assert v == [' ', 'a', 'b'], f'the space is a character too and sorts first, got {v}'

hints: sorted(set(text)) gives a sorted list of the distinct characters.
stoi = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(vocab)} maps each character to its ID. Then [stoi[ch] for ch in s].

problems.title: Count neighbouring pairs
problems.prompt:
BPE starts by counting how often each pair of neighbouring tokens appears. Write count_pairs(ids) that returns a dict mapping each pair (a tuple) to its count.

count_pairs([1, 2, 3, 1, 2])   # {(1, 2): 2, (2, 3): 1, (3, 1): 1}

Neighbours are positions i and i + 1. A clean way to walk over them is zip(ids, ids[1:]), which pairs each element with the one after it.

tests.name: only neighbours count
tests.code:
out = count_pairs([1, 2, 3])
assert (1, 3) not in out, 'only neighbouring tokens form a pair: 1 and 3 are not next to each other'
assert out == {(1, 2): 1, (2, 3): 1}, f'got {out}'

tests.name: repeated tokens overlap
tests.code:
out = count_pairs([7, 7, 7])
assert out == {(7, 7): 2}, f'[7, 7, 7] has two neighbouring pairs (positions 0-1 and 1-2), got {out}'

tests.name: short lists have no pairs
tests.code:
assert count_pairs([5]) == {}, 'a single token has no neighbour, so the result should be an empty dict'
assert count_pairs([]) == {}, 'an empty list has no pairs'

tests.name: finds the most frequent pair in the video's text
tests.code:
t = list('the this that then')
c = count_pairs(t)
best = max(c, key=c.get)
assert best == ('t', 'h') and c[best] == 4, f'in the video t followed by h appears 4 times and wins; you found {best} with count {c.get(best)}'

hints: for a, b in zip(ids, ids[1:]): ...

problems.title: Merge a pair, then train a tiny BPE
problems.prompt:
Write merge(ids, pair, new_id): walk left to right, and wherever pair[0] is immediately followed by pair[1], emit new_id and skip both; otherwise copy the token.

merge([1, 2, 3, 1, 2], (1, 2), 99)   # [99, 3, 99]
merge([7, 7, 7], (7, 7), 8)          # [8, 7]   (left to right, no overlaps)

count_pairs from the previous problem is included, and train_bpe already uses your merge: once it passes, run it on some text and watch common pairs turn into tokens.

tests.name: left to right, no overlaps
tests.code:
out = merge([7, 7, 7], (7, 7), 8)
assert out == [8, 7], f'after merging positions 0-1 the scan continues at position 2, so the result is [8, 7]; got {out}'

tests.name: pair at the very end
tests.code:
out = merge([5, 1, 2], (1, 2), 9)
assert out == [5, 9], f'expected [5, 9], got {out}'

tests.name: last token is kept
tests.code:
out = merge([1, 2, 1], (1, 2), 9)
assert out == [9, 1], f'a lone final token must still be copied (careful with i + 1 going out of range); got {out}'

tests.name: does not change the input
tests.code:
a = [1, 2, 1, 2]
merge(a, (1, 2), 9)
assert a == [1, 2, 1, 2], 'merge should build a new list, not modify ids'

tests.name: BPE shortens text
tests.code:
text = 'the this that then ' * 5
ids, merges = train_bpe(text, 5)
assert len(merges) == 5, f'expected 5 merges, got {len(merges)}'
assert len(ids) < len(text.encode()), 'after merging, the token list should be shorter than the byte list'
assert (ord('t'), ord('h')) in merges, 't followed by h is the most frequent pair in this text, so it should be among the first merges'

hints: Use a while loop, because you sometimes step by 2 and sometimes by 1.
if i + 1 < len(ids) and ids[i] == pair[0] and ids[i + 1] == pair[1]:
Try: ids, merges = train_bpe('the cat sat on the mat. the cat ate.', 10), then print(len(ids), merges).
